e. Geology and Groundwater
(1)Geology
Harrisburg and vicinity is situated in the Great Valley Section of the Valley and Ridge Physiographic Province. Middle Ordovician carbonate rocks with associated younger Ordovician shales underlie the Great Valley throughout southern Dauphin County. Structurally the Great Valley is complex containing numerous thrust faults and structural discontinuities which resulted from gravitational tectonics (changes in the earth's crust).
Carbonate bedrock includes the Hershey Formation, the St. Paul Group and the Pinesburg Station Formation. It consists of dark gray to black, thin, bedded argillaceous limestone, buff colored, even-grained magnesian limestone with layers of chert (a type of quartz), and light gray massive, high calcium limestone.
The greatest percentage of the study area (the general Harrisburg Area) is underlain by the Martinsburg Formation which is a dark gray shale to shaly siltstone that weathers to an olive or brown color. Red, maroon and purple shale, red and olive siliceous shale or chert, aphanitic (fine-grained) dark gray limestone and limestone edgewise conglomerate, sandstone or rounded quartz grains, clayey dolomite, and poorly sorted graywacke (a type of sandstone) occur in minor amounts.
Surficial material incorporates modern alluvial deposits of the Susquehanna River and tributary streams, gravelly silts of higher terraces, and artificial deposits of man such as slag and debris from landfills. Pleistocene outwash terraces are remnants of onetime continous gravel and sand plains laid down by melt waters of Wisconsin glaciation.
A detailed study of the project's geological characteristics has been obtained and is carried in the description of the project which follows later.
